CloverPit is a rogue-like slot machine gambling game. No, there's no microtransactions. You buy the game once with real money but your in-game currency is your soul. You owe money and you're on a Deadline.

You start the game with a few coins and you're allowed to play 3 Rounds of either 3 or 7 spins. At the end of each rounds, you receive Tickets, which you can use to buy Charms at the store. 
Charms will modify almost every aspect the game, be it luck, symbol value, pattern repeating, etc. The store only displays 4 Charms per Deadline and require Coins to reroll the displayed Charms. There's a wide selection, however it's random so expect some chaotic runs.

Once the 3 rounds are up, this ends the Deadline. If you don't have enough coins to pay, this ends the run and you restart at Deadline #1. If you manage to pay up, a new Deadline starts requiring an exponantial amount of Coins to be paid up. The Telephone will ring, providing permanent abilities as well...

Unlock more Charms with each run, find the proper Charm/Telephone combos and [i]pray[/i] you're lucky to win enough Coins to pay your debt before the Deadline ends...

There's no story to talk about, so to speak. You awake in this tiny cell, you're trapped there and you're forced to play this unfair slot machine. There's a voice on the intercom constantly reminding you to pay up before the deadline ends. This may or may not

This is not a game btw, it's a 1:1 simulator of the average evening of any elderly person in Italy after getting their retirement check from INPS.

Here you can experience the generational ritual of "ballarsi la fresca" in first person, and you should be honoured.

The fact that the devs are Italian (I realized that after finding an idol of the Gabibbo as a trinket) just proves that what I wrote above is not just a headcanon, but a documentary.

Firstly, this game has a lot of charms! 160 to be exact. I like the variety and visual design of a lot of them. However, I found myself, especially later in the game, searching for a limited amount of charms every run. There are a few charms that feel like in many circumstances are an absolute necessity for runs to even get far. There are also a LOT of charms that I could never see being used in a real run. Generally speaking, your runs will fall into the pipeline of focusing on a specific symbol through value and occurrence, and also increasing your multipliers. There are a lot of charms that have incredibly rare conditions that you will almost never use, or designing a run around those specific conditions is very difficult to achieve. Which brings me to my next point:

The beginning of every run is very much hit or miss. It is highly dependent on what is in the first or second shop to even get a run going. CloverPit is one of the most unique and addictive indie games I've played in a long time.

I actually played it on mobile first, and I enjoyed it so much that I ended up buying it on Steam as well. There's a surprising amount of content, and the Memory Packs add a lot of variety to each run. The game also has a great selection of interesting items, so experimenting with different strategies never gets old.

I also really like the visual style. The graphics have a unique charm that perfectly matches the atmosphere of the game.

My only real complaint is the lack of background music. The silence can make the game feel a bit empty at times, and I think a soundtrack would have made the experience even better.

Overall, if you're looking for something fresh, fun, and highly replayable, I definitely recommend CloverPit.

Picked up Clover Pit thinking it’d be a quick break game. Big mistake. This thing is dangerously addictive the kind where you say “just one round” and suddenly it’s lunchtime… then somehow also 4PM.

It has that perfect loop: simple to understand, but somehow your brain refuses to let go until you “figure it out” (you won’t). Every run feels like you’re this close to cracking it, which is exactly why you keep going back.

Performance review risk aside, it’s honestly a great pick-up-and-play game. Doesn’t demand too much, but also quietly consumes your entire attention span.

Cons:

HR might become your final boss
Self-control not included

Pros:

Extremely replayable
Perfect for “quick breaks” (lies)

Verdict:
Worth it. Just… maybe don’t install it on your work laptop.

I was initially suspecting lack of depth, but there are a lot of small tricks to learn here to improve the odds. 

That being said, I felt often that the first rounds were the toughest, were you to get unlucky there. Eased a little with practice, but still.

Game starts by not being able to "truly" complete it, so you have to do a few runs to get the full picture. There are also additional modifiers available (20 in total) that change the rules slightly to add replayability.

I unlocked just about everything before posting this, at this point I'd have to grind things like "score 1000 modified sevens" to add couple items to the pool. 

Certain challenge runs are harder than others but I suspect a lot of people, should they aim for 100% completion, will find themselves just going through the motions through many of these challenge runs, as the rules are often not changed in a way that would disrupt regular play "enough".

Was never interested in playing Fruit Machines in my life. This game is amazing, however.  

I felt that I was becoming less and less interested in games because it was like I'd just done it all before. Never going to get that feeling of playing Oblivion for the first time again; GTA Story Mode won't have the same effect it used to have on us. These are experiences we've all had countless times, and furthermore, they have been endlessly copied and re-released, often on a yearly basis. Everyone is doing what is safe and not creative. It becomes incredibly stagnant.

Then come along indie games. Originally stuff like Isaac, Nuclear Throne, Darkest Dungeon, etc. Then Hades happens, and roguelite/indie games get some mainstream spotlight. Everyone is trying to make a game like Hades, and even this space started to stagnate for a moment there.

Enter 2025, the year that broke the mold (again). I've seen so many original ideas this year, maybe something that at a glance you think "WTF even is that?" but if you play it, it just makes sense. It takes all of the things that feel great about playing a roguelite but offers a completely new way of delivering it; it's like scooters to spaceships with the variety, too.

Sorry, this is less a review of this game specifically and more of a general praise to the indie/roguelite scene for the games on my radar recently, Clover Pit being a front runner for GOTY, personally.

Then the next few spins happen. The debt timer gets closer, the machine stops cooperating, and you're staring at the screen wondering how the exact same setup that felt unstoppable a minute ago is suddenly falling apart.

The strange thing is that losing like that doesn't make you want to quit. It makes you spin again immediately just to prove the machine wrong.

And somehow CloverPit is really good at creating exactly that feeling.

This game borrows techniques from Balatro as well as gameplay styles from Buckshot roulette. Combined with some interesting builds from lucky charms to increase how much money you make and various challenge cards to keep you playing, this game does keep you hooked and can be quite addictive. I have spent a lot of time trying to get some insane builds with the charms, some of which I have created on accident reaching as high as E+037 on the money counter.

There is a lot of RNG to this game which has led to my 100% taking so long (Clocked in at 69.5 Hours), however, the developers seem to be updating the game often at the time of writing this introducing patches, as well as the addition of hard mode, balancing it to feel more fair and adjusting lucky charms to be of more use and some to be less broken.

The game feels fun, balanced and the devs seem to care a lot about making this game fun for everyone. I enjoyed the time I had completing all of the challenge cards and collecting all the charms and I will return when there is more content available.

Very fun and addictive roguelike. It seems very "Balatro-inspired" but I would leave the comparisons at just that. Cloverpit is much more RNG-based to the point where it is kind of difficult to compare it with Balatro directly. I fully recommend it either way. Finding combinations of lucky charms that result in big numbers then you'll be entertained. It's not a bad thing that there is even a loose narrative with the game. It keeps you interested in addition to the gameplay.

I felt semi-conflicted the entire time I played this. On the one hand, I love the dark setting and the narrative they're trying to tell about addiction, gambling, and I think capitalism. On the other hand, they use actual tactics of gambling to effectively tell that narrative and I hate that it works on me. I found myself feeling the rush of getting a jackpot, the hollow disappointment when I wasn't hitting at all afterwards, and the pull of risking my cash to get just a bit more if I spin again.

In many ways, Cloverpit feels like the logical conclusion to the recent trend of "indie roguelikes that are basically just gambling without real money" in that it is literally a slot machine roguelike. It gets a bit more of a pass from me for the aforementioned narrative, including the "good" ending, but it's difficult to decide where the line of acceptability is when the actual gameplay is centered on pulling a slot machine.

To be clear - how conflicted and uncomfortable this game makes me feel makes me like it a whole lot more. It reminded me how susceptible we all are to the manipulation tactics of gambling, F2P games using similar tactics, and FOMO-driven purchases.

I will say, though, that once I cleared the "good" ending once, I felt satisfied and dropped it there without unlocking a bunch of of the lucky charms or completing achievements or anything. I haven't gone back after the larger content update and don't know that I will. I feel like I've gotten what I wanted out of

Solid roguelike. Watching your score snowball can be super satisfying, and once you understand the mechanics of the game, it's not terribly difficult to do well in most runs. Getting all achievements takes skill and learning but it's not super grindy.

I will say, I feel like there isn't a whole lot of variety with the strategy and it mostly always boils down to increasing the chances for a specific symbol and going from there. You can't really get anything out of any charms if you aren't getting patterns, and the way to get patterns is to increase the chances of getting the same symbol, so there's no avoiding that really. Even after ~60 hours and getting all achievements, I feel like I was never pushed to explore new strategies, and there are plenty of charms that I never really used, because they never felt strong/necessary. 

All in all, it's fun and I enjoyed completing it, but it's not the next Balatro.
